passages.title: Legal but wrong?
passages.text: Not everything that is legal is ethical, and not everything that is ethical is legal. Tax avoidance is a well-known example. Under no circumstances may a company hide income from the authorities; that would be tax evasion, a crime. However, there is nothing illegal about moving profits to a country with lower taxes, provided that the company complies with the relevant rules. Critics argue that such practices exploit loopholes that lawmakers never intended to create. Defenders reply that companies have a duty to their shareholders and cannot be expected to pay more than the law requires. Between these positions lies a large gray area. Lawyers tend to focus on the letter of the law, while the public is more concerned with its spirit. When the two diverge, trust in institutions suffers. Only when loopholes are closed can the debate move on, but closing them is far from easy. Laws are written in one country, whereas global companies operate in dozens. Moreover, a rule that is too broad may make innocent businesses liable for practices that are perfectly reasonable.

passages.title: The whistleblower's dilemma
passages.text: Imagine discovering that your employer is putting the public at risk. Perhaps the company is hiding safety problems with a product, or falsifying the results of environmental tests. Do you speak out, knowing that you could lose your job, or do you turn a blind eye and hope that someone else will act? This is the ethical dilemma faced by every whistleblower. Some of the most important scandals of recent decades came to light only because an employee was willing to take that risk. Had they stayed silent, the problems would still be hidden today, and many more people might have been harmed. Yet the personal cost can be enormous. Whistleblowers are frequently isolated by colleagues, attacked in the press and forced into long legal battles. Many say they would do the same again; others admit that, if they had known what was coming, they would have kept quiet. In response, a number of countries have passed laws to protect people who report wrongdoing in good faith. Critics argue that these protections are still too weak. If people are expected to put the public interest before their own careers, the law must make that choice a little less costly.
